label: Rollback / back-out plan
title: A “{anchor}” is planned, but nothing describes how to roll it back if it goes wrong
why: Without an agreed way back, a failed “{anchor}” turns into an outage that lasts until someone improvises a fix. Rollback also decides how long the old system must stay available.
question: If the “{anchor}” fails halfway, what is the exact procedure and decision point for going back, and who calls it?
nextStep: Write a one-page rollback runbook with a go/no-go checkpoint and the maximum time you will wait before reverting.
disproof: A document, ticket or runbook that defines rollback or revert steps for the “{anchor}”.

justifications.impact: A failed “{anchor}” with no way back is a full outage
justifications.irreversibility: Data written after the switch may not be reversible
justifications.cost: Mostly a planning exercise: a few hours of writing and a rehearsal

label: Data migration validation
title: Data is being moved (“{anchor}”) but no step checks that what arrived matches what left
why: Silent data loss or corruption is usually discovered weeks later, when reports disagree or customers complain. Reconciliation has to be designed in before the move, not after.
question: How will you prove that every record and total in the new system matches the old one before cutover?
nextStep: Define reconciliation checks (record counts, financial totals, sampled records) and the acceptance threshold for each.
disproof: A reconciliation, validation or parity-check step tied to the “{anchor}”.

justifications.impact: Corrupted or missing records can reach customers and finance
justifications.irreversibility: Bad data that has been used downstream is very hard to unwind
justifications.cost: A few scripted checks and a sign-off rule

label: Load and performance testing
title: The documents state a scale target (“{anchor}”) but never plan a load or performance test
why: Performance targets that are never tested tend to fail on launch day, when fixes are most expensive and most visible.
question: Which test will show the system meets the stated scale target, and when is it scheduled?
nextStep: Add a load-test milestone before go-live, with target numbers taken from the stated requirement.
disproof: A test plan, milestone or ticket for load, stress or performance testing.

justifications.impact: Slow or failing system at launch
justifications.irreversibility: Architecture changes late in the project are costly
justifications.cost: Needs test environment and tooling, but is routine

label: Security review
title: The system handles “{anchor}”, but no security review or penetration test is planned
why: Systems that touch credentials, personal data or payments attract the most scrutiny. Findings discovered after launch can force emergency changes or disclosure.
question: Who will review the “{anchor}” handling for security issues before launch, and what would block the release?
nextStep: Schedule a threat-modelling session now and an external penetration test before go-live.
disproof: A security review, threat model or penetration-test plan covering the “{anchor}” handling.

justifications.impact: A breach or audit failure is existential for trust
justifications.irreversibility: Disclosure and incident response cannot be undone
justifications.cost: Needs budget for an external test and a few days to fix issues

label: Monitoring and alerting
title: Going to production (“{anchor}”) is planned, but nothing says how failures will be detected
why: Without monitoring, the first sign of a problem is a customer complaint. Alert thresholds and on-call ownership have to exist before launch.
question: What will tell the team within minutes that something is wrong after “{anchor}”, and who gets paged?
nextStep: List the 5-10 signals that matter, set alert thresholds, and name the on-call owner for the first two weeks.
disproof: A monitoring, alerting, logging or on-call plan for the production system.

justifications.impact: Outages last longer and cost more
justifications.irreversibility: Detection gaps can be fixed later, but damage before detection cannot

label: Backup and disaster recovery
title: The plan depends on a production data store (“{anchor}”) but never mentions backups or recovery targets
why: If data is lost or corrupted, the only protection is a backup that has actually been restored. Recovery time and acceptable data loss (RPO/RTO) are business decisions.
question: How much data can the business afford to lose and how fast must service return, and has a restore been tested?
nextStep: Agree RPO and RTO with the business owner and schedule a restore test before launch.
disproof: A backup, restore, RPO/RTO or disaster-recovery statement.

justifications.impact: Permanent data loss ends the product
justifications.irreversibility: A lost dataset cannot be recreated
justifications.cost: Mostly configuration plus one restore drill

label: Training and change management
title: People will have to change how they work (“{anchor}”), but no training or adoption plan appears
why: New systems fail through low adoption as often as through bugs. Training and communication need lead time that rarely fits at the end of a schedule.
question: Who needs to learn what before “{anchor}”, how will they be trained, and who answers questions in the first month?
nextStep: List the affected roles, draft a training and communications plan, and reserve time for it before go-live.
disproof: A training, enablement or communications plan for the “{anchor}”.

justifications.irreversibility: Habits that form around workarounds are hard to reverse

label: Privacy and data protection
title: The project processes “{anchor}”, but retention, consent and legal basis are not addressed
why: Privacy obligations attach to the data, not the project. Gaps surface in audits or customer due-diligence and can block launch in some markets.
question: What is the legal basis, retention period and data location for the “{anchor}”, and who signed it off?
nextStep: Run a short data-protection impact check and record the answers in the project documents.
disproof: A privacy, retention, consent or data-protection section covering the “{anchor}”.

justifications.impact: Fines, blocked launches and lost enterprise deals
justifications.irreversibility: Data already collected without basis is difficult to remediate
justifications.cost: Needs legal input; weeks rather than days

label: Vendor and licence exit terms
title: The plan relies on a “{anchor}” but no exit, renewal or data-export terms are mentioned
why: Contract dates and exit terms often drive the real schedule. Missing a notice period can mean paying for a system you have already replaced.
question: What are the notice period, renewal date and data-export rights in the “{anchor}”, and do they fit the project timeline?
nextStep: Pull the renewal and notice dates from the contract and put them on the project timeline.
disproof: A contract clause, date or note about exit, renewal or export for the “{anchor}”.

justifications.impact: Unplanned spend or loss of access to data

label: Support handover and hypercare
title: After “{anchor}” someone has to run the system, but no runbook, support model or hypercare period is defined
why: The team that builds a system is rarely the team that supports it. Without a handover, the first incidents land on whoever is nearest.
question: Who owns incidents after “{anchor}”, what do they need to know, and how long does the project team stay on call?
nextStep: Define the support model, write a runbook, and plan 2-4 weeks of hypercare.
disproof: A runbook, handover, hypercare or support-model description for after “{anchor}”.

justifications.impact: Slow incident response in the first weeks
justifications.irreversibility: Reputation damage is hard to repair
justifications.cost: A short workshop and a document

label: Feature parity with the system being replaced
title: The plan replaces or retires an existing system (“{anchor}”), but no inventory says which features must be kept
why: Legacy systems carry undocumented behaviour that users depend on. Unlisted features are found after cutover, when users cannot work.
question: Which behaviours of the existing system are still used, and which will be dropped on purpose?
nextStep: Inventory features and reports in use (from logs and interviews) and mark each keep, change or drop.
disproof: A feature inventory, parity matrix or list of intentionally dropped features.

justifications.impact: Users blocked on day one of the new system
justifications.irreversibility: Dropped features can be rebuilt but at emergency cost
